lead: Design aids are tables and charts that solve the flexure equations once for every case, so a designer reads the steel instead of solving a quadratic. The Indian set is SP 16, Design Aids for Reinforced Concrete to IS 456. You enter a table with M<sub>u</sub>/bd² and read the steel percentage p<sub>t</sub>. Only a few universities teach the aids as a topic, but many allow SP 16 in the exam hall, and using it correctly saves ten minutes on a design question.
prereq: You need the Annex G steel formula of singly reinforced beams.

blocks.text: Divide the Annex G equation by b d² and both sides become stresses in N/mm²: M<sub>u</sub>/bd² depends only on p<sub>t</sub>, f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>. Solving for p<sub>t</sub> gives the formula every flexure table prints:

blocks.where: p<sub>t</sub> is the tension steel as a percentage of b d; M<sub>u</sub>/bd² is in N/mm² with M<sub>u</sub> in N·mm and b, d in mm.

items: Tables 1 to 4: p<sub>t</sub> for singly reinforced sections, one table per concrete grade (f<sub>ck</sub> = 15, 20, 25, 30), with columns for the steel grades. Charts 1 to 4 plot the same values as curves.
Tables C, D and E: the limiting values x<sub>u,max</sub>/d, M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd² and p<sub>t,lim</sub>; each singly reinforced table ends at M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd² (3.45 N/mm² for M25 with Fe415).
Table F: the compression steel stress fsc against d′/d (doubly reinforced beams).
Tables 45 to 56: p<sub>t</sub> and p<sub>c</sub> for doubly reinforced sections, for four values of d′/d up to 0.2, three steel grades and four concrete grades.

blocks.text: The row above is computed from the formula; it is what the M25 table gives for Fe415. The last row of that table is p<sub>t,lim</sub> = 1.20 % at M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd² = 3.45 N/mm².

items: Put M<sub>u</sub> in N·mm and b, d in mm; compute M<sub>u</sub>/bd².
Check it against M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd² for the grades. If it is larger, go to the doubly reinforced tables.
Open the table for your f<sub>ck</sub>, the column for your f<sub>y</sub>, and read p<sub>t</sub>, interpolating between rows.
A<sub>st</sub> = p<sub>t</sub> b d/100; choose bars.

blocks.text: For a doubly reinforced section the same idea gives p<sub>c</sub> = 100 (M<sub>u</sub>/bd² − M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd²)/[f<sub>sc</sub> (1 − d′/d)] and p<sub>t</sub> = p<sub>t,lim</sub> + p<sub>c</sub> f<sub>sc</sub>/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), which is what Tables 45 to 56 list against M<sub>u</sub>/bd².

examples.question: A beam 300 mm wide with d = 500 mm carries M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kN·m. M25, Fe415. Find the steel with the design aid, then check it.
steps: M<sub>u</sub>/bd² = 150 × 10⁶/(300 × 500²) = 2.00 N/mm², below 3.45 N/mm², so singly reinforced.
The M25 table, Fe415 column, at 2.00 gives p<sub>t</sub> = 0.618 %.
A<sub>st</sub> = 0.618 × 300 × 500/100 = 926 mm². Provide 3 bars of 20 mm (942.5 mm²).
examples.answer: p<sub>t</sub> = 0.618 %, A<sub>st</sub> = 926 mm², 3 bars of 20 mm; the provided bars give 152.6 kN·m.

examples.question: The beam of the first doubly reinforced example (b = 250 mm, d = 500 mm, d′ = 50 mm, M25, Fe415, M<sub>u</sub> = 250 kN·m) is designed with the doubly reinforced aid. Find p<sub>t</sub> and p<sub>c</sub>.
steps: p<sub>t</sub> = 1.197 + 0.174 × 352.1/361.05 = 1.366 %, so A<sub>st</sub> = 1.366 × 250 × 500/100 = 1708 mm², the same as the long calculation.

traps: p<sub>t</sub> is a percentage. p<sub>t</sub> = 0.618 means A<sub>st</sub> = 0.618 × b d/100 = 926 mm², not 0.618 × b d.
M<sub>u</sub> left in kN·m makes M<sub>u</sub>/bd² a million times too small.

Reading the Fe500 column for Fe415: at M<sub>u</sub>/bd² = 3.00 for M25 it gives 0.827 % instead of 0.996 %, 17 % too little steel. Reading the M30 table for M25 changes p<sub>t</sub> only by 4 % here (0.958 %), which is why the steel column matters more.
Using a singly reinforced table beyond its last row, or for a T-beam whose neutral axis is in the web.

quiz.q: What do you enter a flexure table of SP 16 with, and what do you read?
quiz.a: Enter with M<sub>u</sub>/bd² in N/mm² for the given f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>; read p<sub>t</sub>, the tension steel as a percentage of b d.

quiz.q: Why does each SP 16 singly reinforced table stop at a certain M<sub>u</sub>/bd²?
quiz.a: That value is M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd²; beyond it x<sub>u</sub> would exceed x<sub>u,max</sub> and the section would be over-reinforced, so a doubly reinforced table is needed.

quiz.q: b = 230 mm, d = 500 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN·m, M25, Fe415. Find M<sub>u</sub>/bd², p<sub>t</sub> and A<sub>st</sub>.
A table gives p<sub>t</sub> = 0.955 % at 2.90 N/mm² and 0.996 % at 3.00 N/mm². Find p<sub>t</sub> at 2.96 N/mm².
A beam needs M<sub>u</sub>/bd² = 3.90 N/mm² with M25 and Fe415. Give two ways out.
quiz.a: It is above 3.45 N/mm², so no singly reinforced section of that size works. Increase d (M<sub>u</sub>/bd² falls with d²; a 6.5 % deeper beam brings it to 3.44) or use the doubly reinforced tables to add compression steel.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design aids now live inside spreadsheets and design software, which also check shear, deflection and bar spacing in the same pass; the printed tables survive as the quickest check on a computer's answer. SP 16 also has interaction charts for columns, which are used in the column chapter of this subject. Search for SP 16 column interaction charts.

figure.caption: The curve behind the M25 flexure table: entering at M<sub>u</sub>/bd² = 2.00 N/mm² gives p<sub>t</sub> = 0.618 % for Fe415. Each curve stops at its limiting point, 3.45 N/mm² and 1.20 % for Fe415, 3.34 N/mm² and 0.95 % for Fe500.

spec.aria: Graph of steel percentage against Mu over b d squared for M25 concrete, with a solid Fe415 curve, a dashed Fe500 curve, their end points and a read-off at 2.00.
